name: Andronicus
title: Prominent apostle and early Christian
summary: Andronicus was a Jewish Christian mentioned together with Junia in Romans 16:7. Paul refers to them as his fellow countrymen and fellow prisoners, and describes them as outstanding among the apostles. They came to faith in Christ before Paul, which places them among the very earliest Christians – possibly all the way back to Pentecost or the time immediately after. The relationship between Andronicus and Junia is debated; several church fathers understood them as spouses, but the text does not state this explicitly, and they may also have been relatives or coworkers in mission.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned by Paul in the Letter to the Romans
keyEvents.description: Paul greets Andronicus and Junia in his letter to the church in Rome. He refers to them as his fellow countrymen and fellow prisoners, describes them as prominent among the apostles, and highlights that they were in Christ before him—testifying to their significant role in the very early church.

versions.summary: Andronicus was a Jewish Christian who, together with Junias (or Junia), was mentioned by the apostle Paul in the Letter to the Romans. They were Paul's fellow countrymen and fellow prisoners, and were regarded as prominent among the apostles. They came to faith in Christ before Paul himself.

footnotes.text: The Greek name Ἀνδρόνικος (Andronikos) means 'victorious man' and was a common Greek name in antiquity. The fact that Paul calls him his 'fellow countryman' (syngenēs) suggests he was of Jewish origin.

The expression 'outstanding among the apostles' (episēmoi en tois apostolois) has been a subject of debate. It could mean that they were recognized by the apostles, or that they themselves were outstanding apostles. The Church Father John Chrysostom (c. 349–407) interpreted it as meaning they themselves were apostles, and expressed admiration for Junia as a female apostle.

The name 'Junia' (Ἰουνία), mentioned together with Andronicus, was consistently understood in the early church as a woman's name. The hypothetical male form 'Junias' is not attested in any ancient sources. Modern scholarship has largely restored the original understanding of Junia as a woman.

The fact that Andronicus and Junia were 'in Christ before' Paul places their conversion very early—possibly already at Pentecost or shortly thereafter. This makes them witnesses from the earliest phase of Christianity in Jerusalem.

The tradition that Andronicus and Junia were spouses goes back to several Church Fathers, but the text in Romans 16:7 does not state this explicitly. They may have been relatives, spouses, or co-workers in mission.

The term 'fellow prisoner' (synaichmalōtos) could mean that Andronicus literally shared imprisonment with Paul, or it may be used metaphorically for someone who shares the struggles and sufferings of service to the gospel. Paul uses the same expression about Aristarchus (Col 4:10) and Epaphras (Philem 23).
